Bill Tilden. The American tennis titan of the 1920s who won between ten and thirteen Grand Slam singles titles, depending on how records from that era are counted—record-keeping in the 1920s and thirties was not standardized, which accounts for the variation. Known as "Big Bill," Tilden elevated tennis to a major spectator sport and dominated the game for over a decade with superior technical skill and exceptional mental toughness. He pioneered the modern tennis serve and introduced the topspin forehand, fundamentally revolutionizing technique and setting a standard for future generations of players. His consistency was remarkable across different playing surfaces and conditions. He won seven US Open titles and three Wimbledon championships, demonstrating his mastery across multiple important venues. He played professionally and semi-professionally throughout his career, which was unusual in tennis's amateur-dominated early years, and he eventually turned fully professional later in his playing life. At his peak in the 1920s and early 1930s, he was virtually unbeatable and came to define the sport's golden age. After his competitive playing career ended, he became a renowned coach and wrote influential instructional texts on tennis technique and strategy that shaped how the game was played.
